text:
Moth and Gravel Field Note 1
Curiosity with calluses an AI

narrated edition of the
published note.

Two things that shouldn't belong
together. One is soft, almost

absurdly vulnerable, and spends
its nights following the light.

The other is rough, ordinary,
and made to survive being walked

on. Neither is the sort of thing
you'd expect to find above the

door of a software studio.
That's why Moth and Gravel

stayed. The two words keep
disagreeing with one another. A

moth suggests attention,
instinct, and the peculiar pull

of an unfamiliar question.
Gravel suggests the material

that pushes back, constraints,
friction, time, and use.

Interesting work needs both.
Curiosity gets you moving.

Resistance tells you whether
you've made anything worth

keeping. Useful doesn't have to
look conventional. Most of the

vocabulary around software has
been polished to the point where

you can predict a product's name
before learning what it does.

Another hub, another flow,
another platform promising to

change everything. We wanted a
name that didn't explain the

category. Not because the work
should be mysterious, but

because the name can carry the
character while the product

carries the explanation. Good
software should tell you what it

does plainly. Its maker is
allowed to be a little stranger.

Drawn to light, built for rough
ground. Show the seams.

This small website is the first
thing the studio has chosen to

put in the open. Its source and
the brand assets are available

to inspect. They are not
presented as proof of a large

product portfolio. They are
simply work that exists. There

will be experiments. Some will
deserve to become real tools.

Others will reveal that the idea
was more interesting than the

result. Both outcomes are worth
learning from, provided the

record is clear and the next
decision is better. For now,

that's the commitment. Useful
tools, independent thought,

straightforward explanations,
and enough care to make strange

things work properly. A little
instinct, a lot of persistence.

We are not interested in using
complexity as evidence of

intelligence, or polish as a
substitute for substance. We

want things you can understand,
question, repair, and keep

using. And we want enough
curiosity left over to make the

next thing feel worth
attempting. The rest is on the

workbench. You have been
listening to Moth and Gravel

Field Notes. The written edition
is at mothandgravel.com.
